plant_disease_catalog.label: Apple___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Vibrant, uniform leaf color
No spots, lesions, or wilting
Normal fruit development
Strong stems and healthy new growth
recommendations: Maintain consistent watering schedule.
Ensure adequate sunlight and air circulation.
Continue balanced fertilization as needed.
Monitor regularly for any changes.
prevention: Plant in well-drained soil.
Prune regularly to maintain an open canopy.
Provide appropriate spacing between trees.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Target_Spot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A fungal disease that affects all above-ground parts of the tomato plant, characterized by lesions with concentric rings.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint, water-soaked spots on upper leaf surfaces.
Lesions enlarge and develop dark, concentric circles, resembling a target.
Yellow halos may form around lesions.
Fruit lesions are slightly sunken, brown flecks that enlarge into sunken craters with concentric circles.
recommendations: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, or boscalid.
Begin applications before symptoms appear if conditions are favorable (high humidity, leaf wetness).
Remove and destroy heavily infected plant debris.
prevention: Rotate crops, avoiding tomato and other hosts for at least 3 years.
Improve airflow through wider plant spacing and pruning.
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation.
Manage weeds, which can be alternate hosts.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus
plant_disease_catalog.description: A highly stable and infectious plant virus that causes mottling of leaves and distortion, significantly reducing fruit set and quality.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic or mottle on leaves.
Leaves may appear 'fern-like' with pointed tips or be twisted and distorted.
Plants may be dwarfed or stunted.
Fruit may be distorted, show yellow blotches, or have internal browning.
recommendations: There is no chemical cure for infected plants.
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread.
Disinfect all tools, stakes, and hands with a strong soap or bleach solution after handling infected plants.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (check seed packets for 'ToMV' resistance).
Use certified virus-free seed.
Wash hands and tools thoroughly before handling plants, especially if you use tobacco products (TMV, a related virus, is common in tobacco).
Control weeds, as they can host the virus.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Leaf_Mold
plant_disease_catalog.description: A fungal disease that primarily affects tomato leaves, common in high-humidity environments like greenhouses and hoophouses.
symptoms: Pale green or yellowish spots on the upper leaf surface.
Olive-green to brown velvety, spore-filled patches on the *underside* of the leaf, corresponding to the yellow spots above.
Infected leaves eventually turn yellow, wither, and die.
Can cause flowers to drop but rarely affects fruit directly.
recommendations: Apply fungicides, but control is difficult and prevention is key.
Improve air circulation dramatically by pruning and spacing plants.
Reduce humidity by venting greenhouses or hoophouses.
Water in the morning so foliage can dry quickly.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (many greenhouse varieties have resistance).
Ensure wide plant spacing for good airflow.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant.
Sanitize greenhouse structures and stakes between seasons.
common_confusion: Powdery Mildew (which is usually white and on top of leaves)
Late Blight (which has greasy, dark lesions)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Late_blight
plant_disease_catalog.description: A highly destructive disease of tomatoes and potatoes, capable of destroying entire fields rapidly under cool, moist conditions.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked spots (lesions) on leaves, often with a pale green or gray border.
A fuzzy white mold may appear on the *underside* of leaves around the lesions in high humidity.
Stems develop large, dark brown to black lesions.
Fruit develops large, firm, brown, oily-appearing blotches.
recommendations: Preventative fungicide application is critical. Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper compounds *before* disease appears or at first sign.
Once established, it is extremely difficult to control.
Remove and destroy infected plants and any volunteer tomato/potato plants immediately. Do not compost.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties, if available.
Ensure good airflow and spacing.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water soil directly.
Remove and destroy any nearby volunteer tomato or potato plants, as they harbor the pathogen.
Rotate crops; do not plant tomatoes where potatoes were.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot)
plant_disease_catalog.description: A fungal disease characterized by irregular spots on grape leaves, which can cause premature defoliation, weakening the vine.
symptoms: Large, irregular-shaped spots on leaves, often dull red to brown or black.
Spots may turn black and brittle with age.
In severe cases, lesions merge, and the central portion may fall out, giving a 'shot-hole' appearance.
Can cause premature leaf drop, which reduces fruit quality and winter hardiness.
recommendations: Apply protective fungicides. Fungicide programs aimed at managing Black Rot or Downy Mildew (e.g., mancozeb, captan) are often effective.
Rake and destroy fallen leaves to reduce overwintering inoculum.
prevention: Promote good air circulation through proper pruning and vine training.
Practice good sanitation by removing and destroying fallen leaf debris in the fall.
Ensure balanced plant nutrition.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A serious bacterial disease of peppers and tomatoes that causes spots on leaves and fruit, leading to defoliation and unmarketable fruit.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on the underside of leaves.
Spots enlarge, turn brown to black with a greasy appearance, and may have a yellow halo.
Leaf spots may fall out, creating a 'shot-hole' look.
Severe infection leads to yellowing and significant leaf drop (defoliation).
Fruit lesions appear as small, raised, brown-to-black scabs or warts, making fruit unmarketable.
recommendations: Preventative sprays with copper-based bactericides (e.g., copper hydroxide) mixed with mancozeb can provide partial control.
Once established, chemical control is very difficult.
Avoid handling plants when they are wet.
Remove and destroy infected plant debris.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (look for 'BLS' resistance codes).
Use certified pathogen-free seed and transplants.
Practice crop rotation (at least 1 year without peppers or tomatoes).
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation.
Sanitize all tools, stakes, and equipment.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Grape___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Vibrant, uniform leaf color
No spots, lesions, or wilting
Full, healthy fruit clusters
Strong canes and healthy new growth
recommendations: Maintain consistent watering schedule.
Ensure adequate sunlight and air circulation through proper trellising.
Continue balanced fertilization as needed.
Monitor regularly for any changes.
prevention: Plant in well-drained soil.
Prune annually during dormancy to manage canopy and fruit load.
Practice good weed control.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_spot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A major foliar disease of corn worldwide, characterized by rectangular lesions that reduce photosynthetic area and can cause significant yield loss.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint lesions with yellow halos, starting on lower leaves.
Lesions mature into long, narrow, rectangular, tan or gray spots.
Spots are 'vein-limited', meaning they are restricted by the parallel leaf veins, giving them a blocky shape.
Lesions can merge, blighting large areas of the leaf and killing it.
recommendations: Apply foliar fungicides, especially if the disease is present on upper leaves at or before tasseling. Common active ingredients include strobilurins (e.g., azoxystrobin) and triazoles (e.g., tebuconazole).
Scout fields regularly, especially in continuous corn and no-till systems.
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant hybrids (the most effective method).
Practice crop rotation (rotate away from corn for at least one year).
Manage residue using tillage to break down the debris where the fungus overwinters.
common_confusion: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (lesions are larger, 'cigar-shaped')

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Vibrant, uniform green leaves
No spots, lesions, or wilting
Normal fruit set and development
Sturdy stems and vigorous new growth
recommendations: Maintain consistent watering schedule, watering at the base.
Ensure adequate sunlight.
Provide support (stakes or cages).
Monitor regularly for pests and diseases.
prevention: Plant in well-drained, nutrient-rich soil.
Mulch to prevent soil splash.
Ensure good air circulation through pruning and spacing.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Bacterial_spot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A serious bacterial disease of tomatoes and peppers that causes spots on leaves and fruit, leading to defoliation and unmarketable fruit.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown to black.
Lesions often have a yellow halo.
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop, leading to defoliation.
Fruit spots are small, dark, raised, and scab-like.
Unlike on pepper, fruit lesions on tomato are typically flat or slightly raised, not warty.
recommendations: Preventative sprays with copper-based bactericides (e.g., copper hydroxide) mixed with mancozeb can provide partial control.
Once established, chemical control is very difficult.
Avoid handling plants when they are wet.
Remove and destroy infected plant debris.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Use certified pathogen-free seed and transplants.
Practice crop rotation (at least 1 year without peppers or tomatoes).
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation.
Sanitize all tools, stakes, and equipment.
common_confusion: Bacterial Speck (spots are smaller, black, and flat)
Septoria Leaf Spot (fungal spots have tan centers)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening)
plant_disease_catalog.description: One of the most severe and destructive citrus diseases worldwide. It is spread by an insect (the Asian citrus psyllid) and is currently incurable, leading to tree decline and death.
symptoms: Asymmetrical chlorosis (blotchy mottle) on leaves; one side of the leaf may be yellow while the other is green.
Yellow shoots and vein yellowing.
Leaves may be small, upright, and show symptoms resembling zinc or manganese deficiency.
Fruit is small, lopsided/asymmetrical, and fails to color properly (remains green at one end).
Fruit has a salty, bitter taste. Significant premature fruit drop.
Eventual twig dieback and tree death.
recommendations: There is no cure for HLB.
Infected trees must be removed and destroyed to prevent further spread.
Intensive insecticide programs are used to control the Asian citrus psyllid (the vector).
Enhanced nutritional programs (foliar feeds) can help symptomatic trees remain productive for a short time but will not cure them.
prevention: Use only certified disease-free nursery stock.
Aggressively control the Asian citrus psyllid vector.
Scout orchards frequently and remove any symptomatic trees immediately.
Do not move citrus plant material between regions.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight
plant_disease_catalog.description: A common and potentially serious fungal disease of corn, characterized by large, cigar-shaped lesions on the leaves, which can significantly reduce yield if infection occurs before silking.
symptoms: Large (1 to 7 inches long), elliptical, 'cigar-shaped' lesions.
Lesions are tan or grayish and run parallel to leaf margins.
Under humid conditions, lesions may have a dark, 'dirty' or sooty appearance from fungal spores.
Lesions start on lower leaves and move up the plant.
Can coalesce to blight entire leaves.
recommendations: Apply foliar fungicides (strobilurins, triazoles) if disease is present, especially if infection reaches the ear leaf or higher around the tasseling stage.
Scout fields to determine disease severity.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids (most effective method).
Practice crop rotation (rotate away from corn for at least one year).
Manage residue using tillage to break down corn debris where the fungus overwinters.
common_confusion: Gray Leaf Spot (lesions are smaller, rectangular, vein-limited)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Potato___Late_blight
plant_disease_catalog.description: A highly destructive disease of potatoes and tomatoes, famous for causing the Irish Potato Famine. It can destroy entire fields rapidly under cool, moist conditions.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked spots (lesions) on leaves, often with a pale green or gray border.
A fuzzy white mold may appear on the *underside* of leaves around the lesions in high humidity.
Stems develop large, dark brown to black lesions.
Tubers develop a brown, corky, dry rot that extends into the flesh. The surface may be sunken and purplish.
recommendations: Preventative fungicide application is critical. Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper compounds *before* disease appears.
Once established, it is extremely difficult to control.
Remove and destroy infected plants and any volunteer tomato/potato plants immediately. Do not compost.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes.
Plant resistant varieties.
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potato/tomato plants.
Ensure good airflow and avoid overhead irrigation.
Rotate crops; do not plant potatoes where tomatoes were.
common_confusion: Early Blight (has 'target' rings, not white mold)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Blueberry___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Lush, green leaves (may have reddish fall color)
No spots, lesions, or powdery mildew
Plump, healthy berries
Vigorous new cane growth
recommendations: Maintain acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5).
Provide consistent moisture; blueberries have shallow roots.
Fertilize with products for acid-loving plants.
Monitor for pests and diseases.
prevention: Plant in full sun in well-drained, acidic soil.
Mulch with pine bark or needles to retain moisture and maintain pH.
Prune annually to remove old canes and improve air circulation.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Apple___Apple_scab
plant_disease_catalog.description: A common and serious fungal disease of apples, causing lesions on leaves and fruit, which can make fruit unmarketable and weaken the tree.
symptoms: Olive-green to black, velvety or fuzzy spots on leaves.
Leaves may become distorted, puckered, and turn yellow, dropping prematurely.
Fruit spots are dark, 'scabby', corky, and often cracked.
Early fruit infections can cause fruit to be deformed and drop.
recommendations: Apply fungicides preventatively, starting from the 'green tip' stage in spring until dry weather prevails.
Common fungicides include captan, mancozeb, and sterol inhibitors (e.g., myclobutanil).
Prune trees to open the canopy, promoting faster drying.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, GoldRush).
Rake up and destroy fallen leaves in the fall to remove the overwintering fungus.
Applying urea to fallen leaves in fall can speed up decomposition.
Prune for good air circulation.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Corn_(maize)___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Broad, green leaves without spots or streaks
Sturdy, strong stalk
Well-formed ears with full kernel set
Healthy root system
recommendations: Maintain appropriate nutrient levels, especially Nitrogen.
Ensure consistent watering, especially during pollination.
Monitor for pests (e.g., corn earworm, stalk borer).
Scout for early signs of disease.
prevention: Plant high-quality, disease-resistant hybrids.
Use appropriate plant spacing for your hybrid and region.
Practice crop rotation.
Maintain good weed control.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles)
plant_disease_catalog.description: A complex fungal trunk disease that can kill vines slowly (chronic form) or suddenly (apoplexy). It rots the wood from the inside out.
symptoms: Chronic: 'Tiger-stripe' pattern on leaves (interveinal chlorosis/reddening followed by necrosis).
Chronic: Small, dark spots on berries, often with a purple border ('black measles').
Acute ('Apoplexy'): Sudden wilting and death of the entire vine, often in mid-summer.
Cross-section of the trunk or cane shows dark-brown vascular streaking or a central white, spongy rot.
recommendations: There are no effective chemical cures for an established infection.
Infected cordons or trunks should be surgically removed by cutting back to healthy, un-streaked wood.
Remove and destroy dead vines.
Protect pruning wounds with a sealant or fungicide (e.g., Trichoderma-based products) immediately after pruning.
prevention: Protect all pruning wounds, especially large ones, from infection.
Avoid pruning during heavy rain when spores are easily spread.
Sanitize pruning tools between vines.
Double-prune (make a rough cut, then a final cut) to help wounds heal.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Strawberry___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Typically three-parted, vibrant green leaves.
No spots or scorching.
Plump, fully colored, and unblemished fruit.
Healthy crown and runner production.
recommendations: Maintain consistent moisture.
Fertilize with a balanced fertilizer.
Monitor for pests (e.g., spider mites, slugs).
Renovate beds after harvest (for June-bearing types).
prevention: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil.
Use straw mulch to keep fruit off the soil and reduce weeds.
Ensure good air circulation with proper spacing.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_
plant_disease_catalog.description: A fungal disease favored by cool, moist conditions. It rarely causes significant yield loss in modern field corn hybrids but can be an issue in sweet corn or seed corn.
symptoms: Small, oval or elongated, powdery, brick-red to cinnamon-brown pustules.
Pustules erupt through the leaf surface.
Pustules are found scattered on *both* the upper and lower leaf surfaces.
As pustules age, they turn black.
recommendations: Fungicide application is not typically warranted for field corn, as most hybrids have good resistance.
For highly susceptible sweet corn or seed corn, fungicides (strobilurins, triazoles) can be effective if applied early.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids (the primary management tool).
The fungus does not overwinter in northern climates; spores are blown in annually from the south, so rotation and tillage are not effective.
common_confusion: Southern Rust (pustules are smaller, orange, and mostly on the *upper* leaf surface; much more severe)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Early_blight
plant_disease_catalog.description: A very common fungal disease of tomatoes and potatoes, characterized by 'target-like' spots. It typically starts on lower, older leaves and progresses up the plant.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots on lower leaves, 1/4 to 1/2 inch in diameter.
Lesions show a characteristic 'target-board' pattern of concentric rings.
Tissue around the spots often turns yellow.
Stem lesions are dark and slightly sunken.
Fruit can be infected (often at the stem end), showing large, sunken, leathery, black lesions, also with concentric rings.
recommendations: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper compounds.
Begin applications when the first fruit sets and repeat every 7-14 days.
Prune off and destroy infected lower leaves.
Keep plants well-fertilized and watered to reduce stress.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Practice crop rotation (2-3 years) away from tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplants.
Mulch heavily at the base of plants to prevent fungal spores from splashing up from the soil.
Stake or cage plants to improve airflow and keep leaves off the ground.
common_confusion: Late Blight (lesions are larger, greasy, with white mold)
Septoria Leaf Spot (spots are smaller, with tan/gray centers and black dots)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Strawberry___Leaf_scorch
plant_disease_catalog.description: A common fungal disease of strawberries that produces small purple spots, which merge and give the leaves a 'scorched' or burnt appearance.
symptoms: Small, irregular, reddish-purple spots on the upper leaf surface.
The spots do *not* have a tan or white center (unlike Leaf Spot).
Lesions merge, and large areas of the leaf turn purple, then brown, and dry up, appearing 'scorched'.
Leaf margins may curl up.
recommendations: Apply protective fungicides (e.g., captan, strobilurins) starting in early spring.
Remove and destroy older, infected leaves after harvest (during renovation).
Maintain balanced fertility; excess nitrogen can promote a dense canopy.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Use certified disease-free runners.
Ensure good air circulation with proper spacing.
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation.
Remove and burn infected leaves and plant debris in the fall.
common_confusion: Leaf Spot (Mycosphaerella fragariae - has a tan/white center)
Leaf Blight (Phomopsis - has larger, V-shaped lesions)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew
plant_disease_catalog.description: A fungal disease that covers leaves and young fruit with a white, powdery growth, stunting new growth and making fruit unmarketable.
symptoms: Patches of white, powdery, or felt-like fungal growth, typically on the *underside* of leaves first.
Infected young leaves may be distorted, puckered, or twisted.
New shoots can be stunted.
Infected fruit (especially on sweet cherry) develops a white powdery bloom and may be deformed or crack.
recommendations: Apply fungicides (e.g., sulfur, myclobutanil, strobilurins) starting at petal fall.
Horticultural oils can be effective but should not be mixed with sulfur.
Prune to improve air circulation.
Remove and destroy infected water sprouts.
prevention: Plant in a sunny location with good air circulation.
Prune annually to maintain an open canopy.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which promotes susceptible new growth.
Some rootstocks offer more resistance than others.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Squash___Powdery_mildew
plant_disease_catalog.description: A very common fungal disease affecting all cucurbits (squash, cucumbers, melons). It appears as white, powdery spots on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and weakening the plant.
symptoms: White, powdery, circular spots on the *upper* surface of leaves, stems, and petioles.
Spots enlarge and merge, eventually covering the entire leaf.
Infected leaves turn yellow, then brown, and die, exposing fruit to sunscald.
Unlike Downy Mildew, it thrives in warm, dry weather (though it needs humidity to start).
recommendations: Apply fungicides at the first sign of disease. Options include potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, sulfur, or synthetic fungicides (e.g., myclobutanil).
Horticultural oils are also effective.
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (many modern hybrids have PM resistance).
Ensure wide plant spacing to promote airflow.
Plant in full sun.
Avoid overhead watering; water at the base of the plant.
common_confusion: Downy Mildew (yellow spots on top, gray/purple fuzz *underneath*)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider_mite
plant_disease_catalog.description: A tiny, common plant pest (not an insect) that sucks cell contents from leaves, causing a stippled appearance. Populations can explode in hot, dry weather, killing plants.
symptoms: Fine, white or yellow 'stippling' (tiny dots) on the upper leaf surface.
Leaves may appear bronzed, yellowed, or bleached.
In severe infestations, fine, silky webbing is visible, especially on new growth and undersides of leaves.
The mites themselves are tiny (like specks of dust) and are found on the *underside* of leaves.
recommendations: Spray plants with a strong blast of water, focusing on the undersides of leaves, to dislodge them.
Apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil, ensuring thorough coverage of leaf undersides. Repeat applications are necessary.
Use a specific miticide (e.g., abamectin, spiromesifen) for severe infestations.
Release predatory mites (e.g., *Phytoseiulus persimilis*) as a biological control.
prevention: Keep plants well-watered to avoid drought stress, which mites favor.
Regularly spray down plants and paths to increase humidity and knock off dust.
Monitor plants closely, especially during hot, dry periods.
Control weeds in and around the garden, as they can host mites.
common_confusion: Nutrient deficiency (stippling can look like a deficiency)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Apple___Black_rot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A fungal disease that affects all parts of the apple tree, causing a leaf spot ('frog-eye'), limb cankers, and a destructive fruit rot.
symptoms: Leaf Spot: Small purple flecks enlarge into circular, 1/4 inch spots with a tan or brown center and a purple border ('frog-eye leaf spot').
Fruit Rot: Starts at the blossom end (calyx) as a small, sunken brown spot. Rot enlarges in concentric brown and black rings. The fruit eventually shrivels into a black 'mummy'.
Limb Canker: Reddish-brown, sunken areas on bark. Cankers can enlarge, girdle, and kill limbs.
recommendations: Apply fungicides (e.g., Captan, Mancozeb, strobilurins) from bloom through harvest. These sprays often overlap with apple scab management.
Prune out and destroy all cankered branches and dead wood.
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit from the tree and the ground.
prevention: Sanitation is key: Remove mummies, dead wood, and cankers during winter pruning.
Protect trees from stress (drought, winter injury) and other diseases (like fire blight), as the fungus often enters through wounds.
Prune to promote good air circulation.
common_confusion: Apple Scab (leaf spots are velvety, not 'frog-eye')

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus
plant_disease_catalog.description: A devastating viral disease transmitted by whiteflies. It causes severe stunting, leaf curling, and yellowing, and can lead to 100% yield loss if plants are infected early.
symptoms: New leaves are small, crumpled, and curl upwards.
Leaves show interveinal and marginal yellowing (chlorosis).
Plants are severely stunted and appear bushy due to shortened internodes.
Flowers often drop, and fruit production is dramatically reduced or eliminated.
recommendations: There is no cure for infected plants.
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to reduce the virus reservoir.
Control the whitefly vector using insecticides (e.g., neem oil, pyrethrin, or systemic insecticides) and yellow sticky traps.
Rogueing (removing) symptomatic plants is critical.
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties (check for 'TYLCV' resistance).
Use certified virus-free transplants.
Protect seedlings in nurseries with fine mesh netting to exclude whiteflies.
Use reflective mulch (e.g., silver plastic) to repel whiteflies.
Control weeds in and around the field, as they can host whiteflies and the virus.
common_confusion: Physiological Leaf Roll (caused by water stress, leaves roll but are not yellow or stunted)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Potato___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Full, green canopy
No spots, lesions, or wilting
Vigorous growth
Tubers are firm, with unblemished skin and no internal discoloration.
recommendations: Maintain consistent moisture.
'Hill' soil up around the stems as they grow to protect tubers from light.
Monitor for pests (e.g., Colorado potato beetle).
Scout for early signs of Early or Late Blight.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes.
Practice crop rotation (3-4 years).
Plant in well-drained soil.
Maintain balanced soil fertility.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Grape___Black_rot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A serious fungal disease of grapes in warm, humid climates. It can destroy the entire fruit crop by rotting and 'mummifying' the berries.
symptoms: Leaf spots: Circular, reddish-brown spots that enlarge. The center turns tan and is surrounded by a dark border. Small, black, pimple-like dots (pycnidia) appear in the center.
Fruit rot: The most destructive phase. Berries develop small, whitish spots that enlarge. The berry rots, turns black, and shrivels into a hard, wrinkled 'mummy' that remains on the cluster.
recommendations: Apply fungicides preventatively. Sprays should start before bloom and continue until 3-4 weeks after bloom (when fruit becomes resistant).
Effective fungicides include mancozeb, captan, and strobilurins.
Remove and destroy all mummified berries during dormant pruning.
prevention: Sanitation is critical: Remove all mummies from the vine and the ground, as they are the primary source of inoculum.
Prune to promote good air circulation and light penetration.
Choose a sunny, well-drained planting site.
Control weeds.
common_confusion: Esca (Black Measles - spots on berries are different)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Shiny, green, serrated leaves
No spots, shot-holes, or powdery residue
Plump, brightly colored fruit
Healthy bark and new shoot growth
recommendations: Maintain consistent watering, especially during fruit development.
Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest.
Monitor for pests (e.g., aphids, cherry fruit fly).
Net trees to protect fruit from birds.
prevention: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil.
Prune annually to maintain an open, 'vase-shaped' canopy for good air circulation.
Practice good sanitation, removing fallen leaves and fruit.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Peach___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Long, green, vibrant leaves
No spots or 'shot-hole' perforations
Fuzzy, unblemished, and well-formed fruit
Vigorous new growth
recommendations: Maintain consistent watering.
Fertilize in early spring.
Monitor for pests (e.g., peach tree borer, aphids).
Thin fruit in late spring to improve size and prevent branch breakage.
prevention: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil.
Prune annually during dormancy to maintain an open-center canopy.
Apply dormant oil sprays to control overwintering pests.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Peach___Bacterial_spot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A major disease of stone fruits (peach, plum, nectarine) that damages leaves and fruit, causing 'shot-hole' leaves, defoliation, and pitted, unmarketable fruit.
symptoms: Leaf spots start as small, water-soaked, angular lesions that turn purple, then brown.
The centers of the lesions fall out, giving the leaf a 'shot-hole' appearance.
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop, leading to defoliation.
Fruit spots are small, sunken, and dark, often cracking or pitting as the fruit grows.
Small, dark, sunken cankers can form on twigs.
recommendations: Chemical control is difficult. Dormant-season copper sprays can help reduce overwintering bacteria.
Sprays of the antibiotic oxytetracycline may be used during the season, but resistance can be an issue.
Maintain tree vigor with proper watering and fertilization, as stressed trees are more susceptible.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (most important).
Avoid sandy sites, as wind-blown sand can wound leaves and aid infection.
Prune to improve air circulation.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer.
common_confusion: Peach Leaf Curl (leaves are thick, red, and distorted)
Peach Scab (spots are smaller, velvety, and don't fall out)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Pepper,_bell___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Broad, shiny, dark green leaves
No spots, wilting, or yellowing
Firm, well-shaped, and colorful fruit
Sturdy stems and new growth
recommendations: Maintain consistent moisture.
Fertilize with a balanced fertilizer, avoiding excess nitrogen.
Provide support (stakes or cages) as fruit develops.
Monitor for pests (e.g., aphids, pepper weevil).
prevention: Plant in full sun in well-drained, warm soil.
Use mulch to retain moisture and suppress weeds.
Practice crop rotation (don't plant where tomatoes or eggplants were).

plant_disease_catalog.label: Apple___Cedar_apple_rust
plant_disease_catalog.description: A fungal disease that requires two hosts (an apple/crabapple and a juniper/cedar) to complete its life cycle. It causes bright orange spots on apple leaves and fruit.
symptoms: On Apple: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface in late spring.
Spots enlarge and may develop a bright red border.
In mid-summer, small, cup-shaped fungal tubes (aecia) appear on the *underside* of the leaf, directly beneath the orange spots.
Fruit spots are similar, orange and raised, often near the calyx end.
On Cedar/Juniper (Alternate host): Brown, woody, 'golf-ball'-like galls form on twigs. In spring, these galls extrude bright orange, gelatinous 'horns' that release spores.
recommendations: Apply fungicides (e.g., myclobutanil, mancozeb) starting at the 'tight cluster' stage of bud development through the first few weeks after petal fall.
These sprays protect apple leaves from spores being released by the cedar galls.
prevention: The most effective method is to remove all cedar and juniper trees within a 1-2 mile radius (often impractical).
Plant resistant apple varieties.
Prune out and destroy the brown, woody galls from nearby cedar trees during the winter before they produce orange horns.
common_confusion: Quince Rust (similar, but affects fruit more severely)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot
plant_disease_catalog.description: A very common fungal disease of tomatoes that creates numerous small, circular spots on the leaves, leading to severe defoliation from the bottom of the plant up.
symptoms: Many small, circular spots (1/16 to 1/8 inch) on lower leaves.
Spots have a dark brown margin and a tan or gray center.
A key diagnostic feature is the presence of tiny black dots (pycnidia, the fungal fruiting bodies) in the tan center of the spots.
Infected leaves turn yellow, then brown, and fall off.
The disease progresses rapidly up the plant from the bottom.
recommendations: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper compounds.
Begin applications at the first sign of disease and repeat every 7-10 days.
Prune off and destroy infected lower leaves to slow the spread.
Sanitize stakes and cages at the end of the season.
prevention: Practice crop rotation (2-3 years) away from tomatoes or related plants.
Mulch heavily at the base of plants to prevent spores from splashing up from the soil.
Stake or cage plants to improve airflow.
Avoid overhead watering; water at the soil line.
Control susceptible weeds in the nightshade family.
common_confusion: Early Blight (spots are much larger, have concentric rings)
Bacterial Spot (spots are angular, greasy, and lack black pycnidia)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Soybean___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Full, green trifoliate leaves
No spots, lesions, or yellowing (except during natural end-of-life senescence)
Good pod set and bean development
Healthy root nodules
recommendations: Ensure proper soil drainage.
Monitor for pests (e.g., aphids, bean beetles).
Scout for common diseases (e.g., frogeye leaf spot, rust).
Conduct soil tests to ensure proper nutrient levels (P, K).
prevention: Plant high-quality, disease-resistant seed varieties.
Practice crop rotation (especially with corn).
Use appropriate row spacing for good air circulation.
Use seed treatments if planting in high-risk fields.

plant_disease_catalog.label: Potato___Early_blight
plant_disease_catalog.description: A common fungal disease of potatoes and tomatoes, characterized by 'target-like' spots. It typically affects older, stressed plants and can reduce tuber size and quality.
symptoms: Dark brown to black circular spots on lower (older) leaves.
Lesions show a characteristic 'target-board' pattern of concentric rings.
Tissue around the spots often turns yellow.
Lesions can merge, causing large areas of the leaf to die.
Tuber infections appear as dark, sunken, circular lesions with a raised border. The flesh underneath is brown, dry, and corky.
recommendations: Apply foliar fungicides (e.g., chlorothalonil, mancozeb) on a 7-10 day schedule, especially if disease is present and weather is favorable (warm, wet).
Maintain plant vigor with proper fertilization and irrigation to reduce stress.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes.
Plant resistant or later-maturing varieties.
Practice crop rotation (2-3 years) away from potatoes or tomatoes.
Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants.
Do not dig tubers when the soil is wet.
common_confusion: Late Blight (lesions are greasy, water-soaked, have white mold)

plant_disease_catalog.label: Raspberry___healthy
plant_disease_catalog.description: The plant appears to be in good health, free from visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: Vibrant green leaves
No spots, mosaic patterns, or rust pustules
Plump, fully formed berries
Strong, healthy new canes (primocanes)
recommendations: Maintain consistent moisture.
Fertilize in the spring.
Trellis canes to keep them off the ground and improve air circulation.
Monitor for pests (e.g., Japanese beetles, spotted wing drosophila).
prevention: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil.
Prune out old, fruited canes (floricanes) immediately after harvest.
Thin new canes to improve airflow.
Control weeds.
